In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed changes in segregation were driven by a combination of changes in the ethnic composition of schools (and to a lesser extent, of local authorities) and changes in the relative rates of movement of different ethnic groups between the schools and local authorities.

the changing ethnic composition of schools is largely a consequence of the changing composition of the local authority areas from which they draw, and that the changing segregation of schools from one another is a consequence of the same process.

the changing patterns of ethnic composition and segregation in London secondary schools and authorities between 2001 and 2010 were characterized by a process of ethnic polarization, in that the white population became more segregated from both black and Asian populations.

the multilevel random coefficient multinomial logistic model provides a general and flexible tool for the statistical analysis of changing patterns of composition and segregation among multiple groups of individuals across multiple organizational units over multiple occasions, and for re-expressing the model parameters in a wide range of segregation indices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
multilevel multinomial regression is a flexible and powerful tool for modelling the social processes which generate changing patterns of ethnic composition and segregation.

the multilevel random coefficient multinomial logistic model can provide a powerful framework for statistically modelling and interpreting changing patterns of ethnic composition and segregation across multiple groups of individuals and multiple organizational levels over multiple time periods, with the potential to provide a more nuanced and accurate understanding of social processes than is possible with the use of a single segregation index.

the combined multilevel modelling and simulation approach provides a flexible framework within which the social processes which generate changing patterns of composition and segregation among organizational units at different scales can be investigated.
